Look for \(1 - \sin^2 x\), \(1 - \cos^2 x\) or \(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x\), perhaps after taking out a common factor, and replace it using \(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\).

questiondescription.text:
Trigonometry III: simplifying with the identity

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.5: Simplify a trigonometric expression to a single term or a number using sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1.

Core

This question is original to this project.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

falsefeedback.text: Your expression is equivalent, but it is not fully simplified: the answer is a single term or a number. Use \(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\) to replace a group of terms, then tidy what is left.

truefeedback.text: Your answer has the opposite sign all the way along. Test it: at \(x = 60^\circ\) the expression in the question is \({@dispdp(v60,3)@}\), but yours gives \({@dispdp(own60,3)@}\). Check each sign as you replace a group of terms.
